newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Republicans in TV blitz to hold Congress.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Republicans in TV blitz to hold Congress.

text.p: Republicans began a multi-million dollar TV advertising blitz on Monday designed to hold their majority in the House of Representatives in the event Democratic President Bill Clinton wins overwhelmingly.

"What would happen if the Democrats controlled Congress and the White House?" says the ad, launched by the National Republican Congressional Committee barely a week before the Nov. 5 election in about 50 key House districts.
"Been there. Done that. Remember?" the narrator continues.
The ad asserts that a Democratic-run Congress in 1993 and 1994 pushed "the largest tax increase in history ... more wasteful Washington spending ... a government-run health care scheme."
The Republicans regained majorities in both houses of Congress for the first time in 40 years in 1994, riding a tide of discontent with Clinton's early leadership.
They now control the House by 235 to 197 with one independent and two vacancies. Their Senate majority is 53 to 47.

Now concern is spreading in Republican circles that the tide may be about to shift back, what with party presidential nominee Bob Dole running well behind Clinton and many voters apparently feeling the Republican-led House, especially, leaned too far to the conservative extreme.
Many Republican seats gained in 1994 are now fiercely contested by Democrats, sometimes backed by a resurgent organised labour that has spent millions to defeat Republicans.
The new Republican ad tries to play on the labour-Democrat link, saying, "The liberal special interests aligned with Clinton desperately want to buy back control of Congress."?
It then suggests a Democratic Congress would "give the special interests a blank check in Congress."
Craig Veith, spokesman for the congressional Republicans, said the ad would cost "at least $4 million."
Incumbent Republicans are seeking re-election in about half the 50 districts targeted. The other half are open seats.
The last-minute timing of the advertising campaign seemed an implicit acknowledgment that a rout by Clinton might bring down many congressional Republicans along with Dole.
Most analysts and polls suggest the Republican majority is more vulnerable in the House than in the Senate.
Party Chairman Haley Barbour told reporters he expected Republicans to add from one to three seats in the Senate.
He conceded the House situation is more precarious but predicted modest Republican gains there as well. Democrats and some neutral analysts see opposite prospects there.
Barbour said the new ad "reminds people why they are against Clinton" by implying he is a tax-and-spend liberal.

"The ads talk about what Clinton was like when he had a Democrat Congress -- the largest tax increase in American history, a proposal to run a government-run health care system, and Clinton increased federal domestic spending by hundreds of millions of dollars," he said.
But opinion polls give the Republicans cause for alarm.

Asked which party's candidate they would choose for Congress if the election were held now, respondents to a Zogby/Reuters tracking poll taken Friday, Saturday and Sunday picked Democrats over Republicans, 39.2 percent to 35 percent.

In a CNN/USA Today/Gallup poll taken Friday and Saturday, 50 percent of respondents said they would vote for the Democratic candidate in their congressional district while only 43 percent said they would back the Republican.
